articles.full_text:
Mexican judge sentences three men for murders of Australian, US surfers
The trial in Baja California revealed chilling details of the triple homicide of the surfers.
A Mexican judge found three men guilty of the murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in April 2024 in the Mexican state of Baja California.
The trial for the triple homicide that shocked Mexico and drew international attention concluded Friday after Judge Raul Hernandez in the coastal city of Ensenada ruled that Jesus Gerardo Garcia, alias “El Kekas”, Irineo Francisco “N,” and Angel Jesus “N” were responsible for the murders of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and American Carter Redd Rhoad, 30.
The defendants, who had been in custody for more than two years, were also found guilty of armed robbery and armed carjacking.
“Today’s guilty verdict is a significant moment in our long and painful journey to seek justice for our beautiful sons, Callum and Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad, whose lives were so cruelly taken from them in 2024,” said father Martin Robinson.
The three travelled to Baja California in April 2024 to surf and camped near the coastal city of Ensenada, but shortly after arriving in the town of Punta San Jose, about 80 kilometres (50 miles) from Ensenada, they were reported missing. Their bodies were found on May 3 in a well, all with gunshot wounds to their heads.
Garcia, identified as the perpetrator of the murders, was arrested in May 2024 in connection to the case, along with his ex-partner Ary Gisell Silva Raya, Francisco, and Jesus.
During the monthlong trial, chilling details of the brutal crime were revealed. Silva Raya testified last month during a hearing that Garcia confessed to her that he arrived at the tent where the foreigners were staying with a 9mm pistol.
Upon seeing him, they began throwing their belongings to prevent him from attacking them, and one of them begged for his life, which the assailant ignored, she said.
She said Garcia had bragged about “how beautifully” the victims cried and about items he robbed from them.
The state prosecutor’s office reported that Silva Raya arrived in Punta San Jose on April 27, 2024, where she met the three foreigners and “instigated one of her companions to rob them”, which they did the following day.
The woman, who was found in possession of one of the victims’ cellphones, was sentenced in November 2025 to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to “aggravated robbery with violence” and “vehicle theft with violence” in an expedited proceeding. However, Garcia and his two accomplices decided to go to trial.
Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists.
The judge will announce the final sentence on October 16. The Baja California State Attorney General’s Office requested for each defendant the “exemplary sentence” of 210 years in prison.
“No outcome can ever undo this tragedy, but we hope today marks an important step towards justice and allows us to continue honoring their lives and the extraordinary young men they were,” said Martin Robinson. “They will never be forgotten.”

articles.title: Lockheed Martin unveils PAC-3 Edge interceptor designed to counter hypersonic threats
articles.snippet: Lockheed Martin said PAC-3 Edge incorporates a new seeker, upgraded flight controls and a multi-pulse rocket motor supplied by Northrop Grumman.
articles.full_text:
Lockheed Martin on Friday unveiled PAC-3 Edge, a missile interceptor designed to defend against hypersonic and advanced missile threats, as the U.S. military looks to strengthen its capabilities to counter emerging aerial threats.
Growing demand for air and missile defense systems amid conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East has strained U.S. weapons stockpiles, prompting the U.S. Army to award Lockheed Martin a contract worth up to $58.6 billion in July to ramp up production of PAC-3 interceptors.
Lockheed Martin said PAC-3 Edge incorporates a new seeker, upgraded flight controls and a multi-pulse rocket motor supplied by Northrop Grumman, enhancing the interceptor’s ability to counter advanced threats, including hypersonic missiles, at longer ranges and higher altitudes.
“The cost of this would be about that of the existing PAC-3 MSE,” Tim Cahill, president of missiles and fire control at Lockheed Martin, told Reuters. “At full production, the annual rate would be about 2,000 units a year, comparable with PAC-3 MSE.”
In January, Lockheed Martin signed a seven-year framework agreement with the Pentagon to expand production of its PAC-3 missile interceptors, aiming to increase annual manufacturing capacity to 2,000 units from about 600.

articles.title: Lockheed unveils PAC-3 Edge, its next-gen Patriot interceptor
articles.snippet: The aerospace giant intends to invest hundreds of millions of dollars of its own cash in the missile alone, alongside additional investments in its seeker and solid rocket motor, said Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed’s missiles and fire control division.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Lockheed Martin today revealed the PAC-3 Edge, its offering for the Army’s future Patriot interceptor that the company says can fly further and hit more capable targets than the current PAC-3 missile.
Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed’s missiles and fire control unit, said the new interceptor is meant for what Lockheed called the Army’s Future Interceptor program, which he indicated seeks to develop a next-gen version of the Patriot’s current PAC-3 missile segment enhancement (MSE).
Cahill said Lockheed was one of two companies selected to advance in the program. He did not identify the other company, and the Army did not respond to a request for more information today.
Lockheed is set to unveil a full-scale model of the new missile on Monday at the Association for the US Army conference, Cahill said.
“PAC-3 Edge is designed to go after the most stressing targets that we — and, more importantly, that the Department of War — believes are the next-generation [threats] that they’re going to be seeing in the fight from our adversaries,” Cahill said in an interview with Breaking Defense ahead of AUSA, using the secondary name for the Department of Defense.
“PAC-3 Edge will be longer ranged. It’ll be higher altitude. It’ll be more capable to take on targets that are trying to hide,” he added. “It’ll have greater sensitivity in its seeker. It’ll have greater capability to maneuver and to respond to threats.”
Lockheed intends to invest hundreds of millions of dollars of its own cash in the missile alone, alongside additional investments in its seeker and solid rocket motor, Cahill said.
“We’ve already probably somewhere between $50 [million] and $100 million or better put into this,” he said.
Lockheed is developing the seeker in-house, with the intent of being able to use the new technology across other offensive and defensive systems, Cahill said. The company plans to invest about $800 million into the seeker, having invested “several $100 million dollars” into it so far.
For the solid rocket motor, Lockheed is working with Northrop Grumman on a three-pulse motor intended to provide greater range and altitude compared with the legacy PAC-3 missile, he said.
Lockheed intends to begin testing PAC-3 Edge in 2027, ahead of its first deployment in 2031, the company said in a news release.
The PAC-3 Edge will be made on Lockheed’s existing PAC-3 line in Camden, Ark. The company currently is ramping up production of the PAC-3 MSE under an agreement with the Pentagon to triple interceptor production over the next seven years.
To support that effort, Lockheed is building a new MSE production facility outfitted with robotics, automation and AI meant to improve manufacturing efficiency, Cahill said. PAC-3 production will move to the new facility once it’s complete, and the legacy facility will receive the same upgrades.
“That’ll be available then to build Edge in the future,” he said. “Before we ever get to the point where we’re producing Edge, we will have already outfitted the entire factory from end to end with the most modern manufacturing capability available, frankly, in the world.”
The Army has weathered fits and starts in its efforts to develop a next-generation interceptor for the Patriot missile defense system. In 2024, the service announced plans to cancel the Lower-Tier Future Interceptor (LTFI) program, which saw both Raytheon and Lockheed competing to build the new missile.
But a year later, an Army official suggested the program could move forward after all.
“There are some aspects of the LTFI program that are still somewhat pre-decisional, but I believe that we will get support for the program, and I may be in a position this time next year to begin program-of-record execution,” Maj. Gen. Frank Lozano, then the program executive officer for missiles and space, said in October 2025.
“I think right now the glass is probably half full that we’ll get to run that program, and so we’re really in the planning process in figuring out what that’s going to look like moving forward,” he added.
Earlier this year, Lockheed announced the development of the PAC-3 ACE, a less capable, lower-cost version of the MSE that would be available to international customers.
Moving Forward on the Weapons Boom
Since the start of the year, the Pentagon has raced to increase munitions production, inking multiyear framework agreements with weapons makers and suppliers meant to entice companies into modernizing facilities and making major capital investments. Some of those agreements have been turned into undefinitized contract actions, allowing money to start flowing to companies for production.
The department recently awarded Lockheed undefinitized contract actions (UCAs) to ramp up PAC-3 and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) production.
“We were moving forward anyway on our own investment, so we didn’t lose time on that. But clearly the UCAs get us all the contractual authority we need to move forward,” Cahill said. “Definitization of the final contracts — they’ll happen when they happen. Those won’t hold us up.”
Eventually, Congress will need to appropriate the money linked with production increases, but foreign military sales contracts and current domestic orders could help pad out any short-term delays as lawmakers work out the budget, Cahill added.
Lockheed’s partnership with General Dynamics to expand solid rocket motor production is also progressing well, Cahill said. The companies announced the partnership in 2024 with the plan for General Dynamics to produce solid rocket motors for Lockheed’s Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System (GMLRS).
“We just had a motor firing here in the last few days,” he said. “There was a Lockheed Martin-designed GMLRS motor that was partnered with General Dynamics to put propellant in it and to actually fire the motor.”

articles.title: Pentagon, Raytheon sign $6.3B deal to replenish US missile interceptor supply
articles.snippet: The contract "supports urgent replenishment of missile defense inventory that has been successfully used in combat," Raytheon said.
articles.full_text:
The Pentagon inked a five-year contract with Raytheon for the steady production of ballistic missile interceptors that use force to destroy targets, rather than explosives.
The $6.3 billion contract, which provides two additional option years, will see Raytheon provide the Defense Department with a continuous supply of Standard Missile-3 Block IB interceptors manufactured primarily in Tucson, Arizona and Huntsville, Alabama.
“SM-3 Block IB has proven its relevance in combat and this contract helps ensure we can replenish inventories and keep pace with the evolving threats the U.S. Navy, MDA and their partners face around the world,” Raytheon President Phil Jasper said in a statement.
The SM-3 Block IB interceptor belongs to a larger family of “hit-to-kill” SM-3 missile interceptors, which seek and destroy incoming ballistic missiles using sheer speed and momentum.
The Block IB type can be used by land forces and ships and is frequently deployed on vessels due to its range and highly flexible steering. The interceptor tracks flying targets with a two-color infrared seeker and propels itself towards them in short bursts, giving it accuracy at high speed as it homes in on targets.
It is designed to knock short- and intermediate-range ballistic missiles out of the sky when they are halfway to hitting their targets, and has long striking reach. It was used in combat for the first time in 2024 when the U.S. Navy destroyers USS Arleigh Burke and USS Carney fired them to intercept Iranian missiles aimed at targets in Israel.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies named the SM-3 Block IB among “seven critical munitions” in an April report detailing ammunition shortages, alongside Patriot missiles, Precision Strike Missiles, Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missiles, Tomahawk Land Attack Missiles and others.
The contract for more SM-3 Block IBs, announced by Raytheon on Thursday, was among five framework agreements the defense giant signed with the Pentagon this February.
The deal comes at a time when the DoD is seeking to avert diminishing munitions stockpiles. National security specialists, defense analysts and foreign policy pundits cautioned in March that the U.S. military’s increased use of missile interceptors during the war with Iran poses strategic risks to integral defense capabilities if fighting spills into a long-term conflict.
Raytheon stated in its release that the contract for SM-3 Block IB supply “supports urgent replenishment of missile defense inventory that has been successfully used in combat and remains central to protecting U.S. forces, allies and critical infrastructure.”
Zita Ballinger Fletcher previously served as editor of Military History Quarterly and Vietnam magazines and as the historian of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. She holds an M.A. with distinction in military history.

articles.title: US Army activates new multi-domain task force to ‘deny, disrupt’ enemies in Indo-Pacific
articles.snippet: The new 4th Multi-Domain Task Force includes four battalions and is planned to grow to 2,100 soldiers.
articles.full_text:
A new U.S. Army multi-domain task force, one of five recently established or under development by the service, was activated this week with a ceremony at Fort Carson, Colorado.
The 4th Multi-Domain Task Force will focus on synchronizing long-range precision fires in the Indo-Pacific region “to deny, disrupt and disaggregate adversary capabilities” and create advantages for other units in the joint force, the Army said in a release.
The task force includes four battalions and is planned to grow to 2,100 soldiers.
Col. Hugh W.A. Jones assumed command of the task force during Thursday’s ceremony. He previously commanded the 2nd Stryker Brigade, 4th Infantry Division at Fort Carson, leading the brigade when it deployed to the U.S.-Mexico border last year.
“While we build this formation to deter aggression and preserve peace, if war comes, we must be prepared to fight and win,” Jones said during the ceremony. “We owe those in harm’s way every advantage we can give them, while leaving our enemy nowhere to run and nowhere to hide.”
The task force reports to the 7th Infantry Division at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Washington.
In June, the Army combined the 7th Infantry Division and the 1st Multi-Domain Task Force at Lewis-McChord into the 7th Infantry Division (Multi-Domain Command-Pacific), which serves as the multi-domain operational headquarters. Its mission is to integrate “maneuver, fires, air defense, cyber, space, electronic warfare, intelligence, unmanned systems, sustainment and command-and -control in support of the joint force across the Pacific,” the Army said in a release.
Maj. Gen. Bernard Harrington, commander of the 7th Infantry Division, attended the activation ceremony at Fort Carson.
“You are driving the change our nation demands today, to meet the changing character of war, to prevent conflict, and to maintain a free and open Pacific alongside our allies and partners,” Harrington told soldiers assigned to the new multi-domain task force.
The establishment of the 7th Infantry Division (Multi-Domain Command-Pacific) and the 4th Multi-Domain Task Force are part of a broader transformation initiative “to counter near-peer adversaries in an increasingly complex global landscape,” the Army said.
The initiative includes the service establishing five multi-domain task forces by 2028, according to a Congressional Research Service report. The Army activated the 2nd Multi-Domain Task Force in 2021 at the Clay Kaserne installation in Germany, and stood up the third in Hawaii in 2022. A fifth is planned for Fort Bragg, North Carolina.
The units are designed to operate across all domains — land, air, sea, space, cyberspace and information — and “provide combatant commanders with a versatile and potent array of options,” according to the Army.
“As we build this formation, we must never forget that technology earns its value in the hands of well-trained and disciplined soldiers,” Jones said Thursday. “A soldier who solves a difficult problem here may make the difference for an American fighting far beyond the horizon.”
Nikki Wentling is a senior editor at Military Times. She's reported on veterans and military communities for over a decade and has also covered technology, politics, health care and crime. Her work has earned multiple honors from the National Coalition for Homeless Veterans, the Arkansas Associated Press Managing Editors and others.

articles.title: US Army Corps of Engineers failed to explain drop in environmental mitigation work: Watchdog
articles.snippet: A chart published by GAO shows a sharp decline in the agency's decisions to make mitigation plans for wildlife and habitat protection from 2022 to 2025.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers did not seek to mitigate environmental damage for more than 50 projects over the past five years and did not provide detailed explanations to Congress, a government watchdog found.
Measures to prevent environmental damage were proposed in only 22 of 74 civil works projects the Corps submitted to Congress for approval from 2020 to 2025, according to a report published Wednesday by the Government Accountability Office.
The Corps deemed that no such measures were needed for the remaining 52 projects and failed to provide detailed evidence as to why, the watchdog alleges.
The agency regularly works to improve water navigation channels to prevent flooding and restore aquatic habitats around the country through its civil works program. It is required by statute to make detailed reports to Congress outlining whether its projects will require measures to prevent possible harm to fish, wildlife and the environment.
The engineers are expected “to plan for environmental mitigation — that is, to take actions to avoid, minimize, or compensate for expected losses to fish and wildlife and damage to ecological resources,” which could include reinforcing riverbanks or restoring wetland areas to create new habitats for fish and wildlife, according to the report.
The Corps of Engineers may decide not to undertake conservation measures if it deems certain projects will not cause harm. However, the Army is expected to provide Congress with clear explanations for those decisions.
A chart published by GAO shows a sharp decline in the Corps’ decisions to make mitigation plans for wildlife and habitat protection from 2022 to 2025. In 2024, for example, the agency decided that only one of 13 projects would require measures to safeguard the environment.
The GAO’s chart shows zero mitigation plans made in 2025.
In its findings, the GAO alleges that the Corps failed to provide necessary details to Congress demonstrating the reasons behind its decision-making in cases when it deemed no environmental protection measures were needed.
The watchdog said the vast majority of documents sent to Congress during those five years contained broad and general language that failed to clarify how the Corps reached its decisions.
The GAO recommended that the Army establish clear guidance for the Corps to document how it reaches decisions to keep Congress and the public better informed.
The Army disputed the GAO’s recommendations in a Sept. 16 letter signed by D. Lee Forsgren, the senior official performing the duties of the Army’s assistant secretary for civil works.
“We do not concur with the recommendation in the draft that we need to create more guidance about mitigation decision making on Civil Works projects,” Forsgren wrote.
“The water resources project reports (including associated Chief’s Reports) produced by USACE have sufficient technical information for decision makers and the public and resource agencies to understand when habitat mitigation is or is not included in a final recommendation.”
Zita Ballinger Fletcher previously served as editor of Military History Quarterly and Vietnam magazines and as the historian of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. She holds an M.A. with distinction in military history.

articles.title: Official poster depicts the US Army’s newest threat: The Iranian soldier
articles.snippet: The U.S. Army recently published a quick-recognition guide to help soldiers identify members of the Iranian army.
articles.full_text:
If America engages in a ground war with Iran, the U.S. Army wants to ensure that its soldiers can recognize the enemy.
A new U.S. Army poster depicts a soldier of the Iranian army. The graphics show a bearded soldier wearing sunglasses and a beret, with captions describing the various weapons he might carry and the uniforms he might wear.
That the U.S. Army has a quick-recognition guide for Iranian soldiers doesn’t mean America will invade Iran. The Army’s Training and Transformation Command has a library of graphical recognition posters for the armies of various nations, including China’s People’s Liberation Army.
The U.S.’s ongoing conflict with Iran has lasted nearly eight months. For now, both sides have waged war with aircraft, missiles and drones. But the possibility of American boots on the ground has always been present, such as seizing vital Iranian oil facilities on Kharg Island.
The new guide, published Sept. 24, isn’t focused on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the praetorian guard of the Iranian regime that grabs most of the headlines. The IRGC controls many of the weapons that have been fired at American forces and Iran’s neighbors, including ballistic missiles, drones and fast-attack boats.
Instead, the U.S. Army guide displays a soldier of the Islamic Republic of Iran Army, also known as Artesh. It is a mainly conscript force of 350,000 personnel that is essentially the regular armed forces of the nation of Iran, including armored, infantry, special forces, air defense, aircraft and naval units, according to the research organization the Institute for the Study of War.
In contrast, the IRGC protects an Iranian regime that doesn’t fully trust the regular armed forces, which date back to the days of the Shah. As in many authoritarian nations, such as Saddam Hussein’s Iraq, there is a deliberate rivalry between the regular and politicized armed forces, with the regime’s pet army getting the best equipment.
There have been numerous reports of low morale and harsh conditions for Artesh soldiers, including lack of food and medical care. One draftee said in a 2022 essay for the Atlantic Council, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, that most soldiers do menial work, rather than combat training.
The Artesh soldier in the U.S. Army poster — wearing the green beret of the Iranian special forces — doesn’t appear much different than the infantry in many other armies, with a mix of Soviet, Western and Iranian gear. He is shown carrying an AKM, Masaf-2 or Heckler & Koch G3A6 rifle. He can also be armed with an MG3 machine gun or an RPG-7, plus grenades, body armor, rucksack, canteen and gas mask, among other gear.
The image shows five different camouflage uniforms, including khaki and woodland, as well as three camouflage patterns for the special forces. Also shown are the insignia of officer and enlisted ranks.
Michael Peck is a correspondent for Defense News and a columnist for the Center for European Policy Analysis. He holds an M.A. in political science from Rutgers University. Find him at theuncommondefense.com. His email is mikedefense1@gmail.com.

articles.title: Estonia’s KrattWorks crafting Shahed-like dummy drone for target practice
articles.snippet: The Estonian company, which has announced a Shahed-like target drone, will show its products at this year's AUSA conference in Washington.
articles.full_text:
WARSAW, Poland — Estonian unmanned aerial system producer KrattWorks is developing a new aerial target drone that will mimic the operations of jet-powered Shahed-type drones, enabling militaries to practice shooting down one of the main aerial threats used by Russia in its ongoing invasion of Ukraine.
As part of its international expansion plans, the company is promoting its unmanned solutions at this year’s AUSA conference in Washington as it seeks to strengthen its presence in the United States.
The company is pushing the project as numerous anti-drone system producers in Ukraine and other European countries are striving to make their interceptors cheaper than the targets they are meant to strike, and also suitable for mass production using readily available components.
Ranno Pajuri, business development manager at KrattWorks, told Defense News the new dummy drone is expected to be presented by the end of 2027.
“We need to obtain a working prototype that is reliable enough. The good thing is that we have software which can be adapted to different hardware quite easily,” he said. “But if the drone becomes so much different from what we have today and so much faster, then there are many variables to consider before it is stabilized and ready for a demonstration.”
The Ukrainian Army, to which the Estonian company has supplied one-way attack drones as well as other products such as its Ghost Dragon ISR drone, is one of the potential users of the new solution. KrattWorks has delivered its UAVs to customers in Europe, and the company is currently making efforts to boost its foothold in the United States as well as various markets in Asia and Africa. KrattWorks says its Ghost Dragon ISR systems have also been deployed in Estonia, Georgia and Moldova, among others.
“We produce our drones in Estonia. We have enough extra capacity to ramp up the production if the demand will grow. Aerial target drones are usually made within quite a short lead time,” Pajuri said. “But we are open to some level of transfer of production if this is necessary and the demand is large enough in the country to which we are selling our products.”
KrattWorks says its product portfolio includes the DART fixed-wing aerial target, which is intended for use against air-defense missiles, heavy machine guns and anti-aircraft cannons, and the DART-R, an aerial target decoy fitted with a radar reflector that can reach a maximum speed of 200 km/h (124 mph), according to data from the company. KrattWorks also makes the PARM aerial target quadcopter.
The manufacturer said it “builds ISR drones with wide frequency band-hopping radios and GNSS-free flight modes to help first responders and servicemen to gain fast situational awareness in situations where every second counts.”
The business cooperates closely with the Ukrainian Armed Forces and studies the UAV attacks that take place in Ukraine and the evolving tactics used there to improve its products. KrattWorks makes efforts to ensure that its aerial target drones mimic the latest operational trends and act in a realistic manner, the company representative said.
In its September 2026 report on Russia’s use of UAVs against Ukraine, the Institute for Science and International Security, a Washington-based think tank, said the Russian military used an estimated 5,166 Shahed-type drones, including decoys, against Ukrainian targets in August alone.
Meanwhile, the Office of the President of Ukraine said on Sept. 28 that the country’s military had reached an overall drone shoot-down rate of 70%, including both piston-powered and jet-powered Shaheds.
“But for jet-powered ‘Shaheds,’ unfortunately, the rate is much lower than it needs to be – 57%,” the office said in a statement. “New interceptors are being actively tested. Some combat teams are already using them, but of course, some details still need to be refined to ensure sufficient effectiveness and deployment at scale. We are pushing the developers to move faster.”
Jaroslaw Adamowski is the Poland correspondent for Defense News.

articles.title: Century-old houses getting new life at Fort Bragg
articles.snippet: 230 homes built before 1940 are being renovated at Fort Bragg.
articles.full_text:
Homes that are nearly a century old are getting a new life at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, preserving their historic character while providing updated features and addressing safety concerns.
Officials at Fort Bragg and Corvias, the privatized housing company that operates the installation’s housing, recently marked the renovation of the first of 21 historic homes that are ready for military families. They were built between 1928 and 1939, and feature elements including stucco walls, copper gutters, hardwood floors and basements.
Fort Bragg has 230 homes that were built before 1940, and all are designated as historic. But these aren’t even the oldest of Army housing. There are 867 houses built before 1919, located on 19 other Army installations in 13 states and the District of Columbia, according to the Army.
At Fort Bragg, about 2,300 of the base’s 6,104 homes were built before 1960, officials said.
The Army manages the largest inventory of historic housing in the federal government, with more than 30,000 historic homes that are more than 50 years old. These homes are subject to the requirements of the National Historic Preservation Act, according to the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation.
That federal agency’s mission is to promote the preservation of America’s historic places and has worked with the Army and the other services as they prepare plans to renovate these houses, making sure they preserve the historic character while meeting the needs of families.
“These residences are an important part of Fort Bragg’s history, but their greatest value is continuing to serve soldiers and families who live in these homes,” said Col. Luke Wittmer, the installation’s garrison commander, in an announcement. “This renovation preserves history while ensuring we continue to meet the needs of today’s families.”
Historic homes have long been a challenge to preserve and maintain for military families, with a variety of issues such as lead paint and asbestos, which are both hazardous and costly to remediate.
Most of the military’s historic homes were included in the inventory of military housing that was turned over to private companies to operate and maintain, starting in the early 2000s.
According to the Army, historic homes currently take an average of 18 days to prepare between occupants, compared to 15 days for a standard home. The average cost is $4,342, compared to $3,681 for a standard home.
Fort Bragg was designated a permanent Army post in 1922, and construction of the first permanent party officers’ family quarters along Alexander and Hunt streets began in 1927, officials said. Construction of noncommissioned officer family housing began in 1928.
Karen has covered military families, quality of life and consumer issues for Military Times for more than 30 years, and is co-author of a chapter on media coverage of military families in the book "A Battle Plan for Supporting Military Families." She previously worked for newspapers in Guam, Norfolk, Jacksonville, Fla., and Athens, Ga.

articles.title: Pentagon barred Qatar base access to hide Iran war damage, US senator claims
articles.snippet: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., was denied access to Al Udeid Air Base, Qatar, during a recent Congressional Delegation trip in what he calls a "cover-up."
articles.full_text:
A U.S. senator was recently denied access to the largest military installation in the Middle East, calling it a “cover-up” over the damage suffered during the Iran war.
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., visited the Middle East this week on a Congressional Delegation trip, speaking with Gulf region leaders and visiting American facilities to assess damage done by the Iran war. Murphy was denied access to Al Udeid Air Base, Qatar, which had suffered damage from drone strikes during the conflict.
“They are using every tool they can, including withholding information about damages, slow walking the pace of reports about casualties and denying us access to see the damage as part of a campaign of cover-up, so as to mask the true cost of the war,” Murphy told reporters on Thursday.
The “unprecedented” base denial prepared Murphy, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and Defense Appropriations Committee, in the coming days to draft language that would explicitly require the Department of Defense to grant members of Congress access to military bases overseas under all circumstances if needed.
“I don’t have any illusions that that’s going to pass between now and the end of the year, but I think that’ll be a really important part of the discussion around an appropriations bill next year and the defense authorization bill,” he said during the press call.
Prior to his trip, Murphy requested access to the base through a letter and direct appeal to U.S. Central Command leadership. But he was denied access even as the Department of State supported his trip to the region, with the Defense Department saying it was due to previously imposed travel restrictions.
“Senator Murphy’s office was informed before his trip to the Middle East that he would not receive Department of War support to access Al Udeid Air Base, consistent with the Secretary of War’s directive on travel restrictions in the region ordered on March 3, 2026,” a senior Defense Department official told Military Times on Thursday.
“That decision was communicated in advance by the Office of the Secretary of War for Legislative Affairs,” the official continued. “The Department applies the Secretary’s guidance evenly.”
In early March, the State and Defense departments issued travel guidance, calling on Americans to depart areas in the region and updating its travel advisory to recommend against visiting certain countries, including Qatar.
“It is absolutely ordinary for members of Congress to travel to areas of conflict and get to talk directly to the military leaders and the soldiers that are involved in the conflict and see for ourselves the damage that has been done to our bases and equipment,” Murphy said, highlighting how during the Iraq and Afghanistan wars he was able to visit operating bases.
He argued that since Congress decides funding and authorization for war, it is necessary to see the consequences, but he was unable to visit Al Udeid or have a briefing on the war with American military officials while in the region.
On the same day the travel advisory was issued in March, the U.S. embassy in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, was hit by two Iranians drones, resulting in building damage and a fire. Murphy said that the drones impacted multiple floors of the embassy and part of the space is now “uninhabitable” with permanent damage.
The U.S. previously announced in 2023 plans to build a new embassy compound in Riyadh, which Murphy attributes the lack of repairs to.
Even though no injuries or casualties were reported from the strike, Murphy said that if the attack happened during the day it would have killed many Americans.
“[Secretary of Defense Pete] Hegseth is determined to hide the cost and the consequences of this war from the American public, and it is absolutely outrageous that I and Republican senators are being denied the ability to see the damage for ourselves,” he said.
Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

articles.title: Coast Guard places $248 million order for first MQ-9B drones
articles.snippet: The unarmed drones are meant to “give the Coast Guard crews a longer-range view of our maritime domain,” a senior official said.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Coast Guard is purchasing MQ-9B drones for the first time, ordering four of the high-flying unmanned aerial vehicles for just under $250 million.
The aircraft will support the service to oversee offshore waters, conduct search and rescue operations, and help counter drug trafficking operations, among other things, the Coast Guard said in a news release today. They are not expected to carry weapons, a service spokesperson told Breaking Defense.
“The MQ-9B long-range unmanned aircraft systems will expand our reach and strengthen our ability to protect the nation,” Anthony Antognoli, the assistant commandant and program executive officer for robotics and autonomous systems for the Coast Guard, said in a statement. “This investment will give Coast Guard crews a longer-range view of our maritime domain, helping them detect threats earlier, make better-informed decisions and act faster across our missions.”
The Coast Guard first revealed its plans to purchase the drones last year, thanks to funding the service received from President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” that passed in July 2025, Military Times previously reported.
The Coast Guard said today that funding for the MQ-9B acquisition stemmed from the FY25 reconciliation package that included nearly $25 billion for the service, along with FY26 appropriations. The MQ-9B purchase totaled $247.8 million for the four aircraft, along with ground control stations and other supporting equipment, the Coast Guard said.
The Coast Guard has previously teamed up with the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and flown CBP’s MQ-9A drones for operations out of Texas, according to a Coast Guard factsheet. The Coast Guard noted in today’s release that the aircraft supported CBP to seize 60,700 pounds of illegal drugs and the apprehension of roughly 20 “smugglers” in FY26.
The MQ-9B SeaGuardian is designed to conduct maritime intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance operations for more than 30 hours at a time with a mission radius of roughly 1,200 nautical miles, according to General Atomics, which builds the aircraft.

articles.title: One year in, Army’s FUZE leader eyes ‘bigger’ acquisition challenges
articles.snippet: The Army innovation hub’s first year also revealed the challenge of making sure promising technologies don’t stop at the prototype stage, FUZE Director Matt Willis told Breaking Defense.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — After a first year focused on adapting prototype technologies for military use, the Army’s FUZE innovation hub is setting sights on more complex acquisition challenges in fiscal 2027.
“A lot of what we’ll see in FY27 is leveraging mechanisms within the Army FUZE portfolio to address bigger Army acquisition problems, and I think again this demonstrates that the Army recognizes we need to diversify the defense industrial base,” FUZE Director Matt Willis told Breaking Defense in an interview last month.
Established in September 2025 by then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, FUZE is the service’s flagship venture-capital innovation engine designed to accelerate deployment of new technologies using pre-existing acquisition mechanisms. The office falls under the Army’s Pathway for Innovation and Technology (PIT) portfolio, which is facilitated by the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Acquisition, Logistics and Technology office.
According to Willis, the organization’s overall goal is to find new tech and deliver it to the warfighter faster. But FUZE’s first year also showed the challenge of making sure promising technologies don’t stop at the prototype stage where they can fall into the ever-dreadful tech valley of death.
That prompted the organization to focus on getting Army acquisition officials involved earlier to create a clearer path toward procurement in FY27, he said.
“We need to incentivize innovation, and we need to invest in emerging or bleeding-edge capabilities to stay ahead of the rapidly evolving threat landscape … or how fast war is changing. We can see that in Ukraine and elsewhere,” Willis said.
Igniting the FUZE
Broadly, the PIT acts as a “plus one” structure in tandem with the Army’s six Portfolio Acquisition Executives (PAEs), bringing together multiple offices focused on fielding emerging capabilities. All organizations within the PIT are geared toward harnessing innovation and getting tech to the warfighter sooner, but FUZE specifically uses a venture-capital style model to do so.
FUZE is allocated $750 million in annual, “non-dilutive” research, development, test and evaluation (RDT&E) funds. The money is pulled together from four existing innovation efforts — xTech, Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) Programs, the Technology Maturation Initiative and the Army Manufacturing Technology Program.
Before FUZE, the four funding streams were dispersed throughout the Army, making it difficult for companies to understand how to acquire funding for a promising capability, Willis said.
“The big piece and the power of the Army FUZE program is this sort of continuity, or seamlessness — or as seamless as we can make it in the government,” Willis said.
First, companies demonstrate their capabilities during Army xTech competitions and if they are placed among the top contenders they win a cash prize. Then, the SBIR program gives those vendors additional money to develop initial prototypes, while the TMI funding helps with “scaling that prototype,” Willis said. The final step is securing the ManTech investment, which vendors use to reduce manufacturing costs.
Once this process is complete, the Army’s network of venture and private capital partners “inject” funding into the companies so they can eventually scale their products and get on contract with the service through the PAEs, Willis explained.
“This has really been foundational in terms of bridging the gap between [the Army’s] mission needs and private sector venture capital,” he said. “Rather than expecting startups to just rely solely on government R&D funding, we’re actively signaling defense priorities to private markets.”
But FUZE is still refining the process to ensure vendors come out with a contract instead of a box full of prototypes, he said. To achieve this, the office wants to engage with PAEs from the outset to ensure there’s a clear pathway for tech to advance.
“I’d say we’re doubling down or tripling down on this sort of mandate that, for all of our FUZE investments — for all the project investments that we’re making — we’re building in this piece where we have buy-in from the warfighting unit,” Willis said.
Drones Dominate, EW Less So
FUZE held about 16 xTech competitions in fiscal 2026 focused primarily on drones, counter-drone systems, electronic warfare and energy resiliency. Willis said the office “exceeded” its goal of getting capabilities into the field within 60 to 75 days of posting a solicitation — a process that can traditionally take several months or even years.
In some cases, the organization was able to go from a solicitation to contracts in less than five days. All four technology areas have made it into the field in some capacity, meaning the tech was either delivered to a unit for permanent use or as part of a “soldier experimentation event,” Willis said.
Vendors were more receptive to some capabilities than others, with drone and counter-drone tech being the most popular among industry, Willis said.
“The commercial sector is already mass producing these platforms at high volume, and what we’re looking for in the Army is not starting with basic research and matriculating all the way up through a prototype,” he said. “Then a big piece for us from an adaptation perspective is — how can we make them military grade?”
By contrast, electronic warfare drew less industry interest because “it has the least overlap with commercial applications,” Willis said. As for energy resiliency capabilities, FUZE has provided some solutions to the field, but it’s still “definitely the latest push,” he added.
FUZE now wants to tackle more challenging acquisition problems, including low-cost interceptors. While these systems are not considered widely commercially available or affordable, they can be built using off-the-shelf, inexpensive components, Willis explained.
To kickstart the effort, FUZE launched the xTech Disrupt Fires competition to search for a second low-cost interceptor for the Army’s Indirect Fire Protection Capability (IFPC) Increment 2 program specifically designed to hit low-flying and supersonic targets.
During the annual AUSA conference this year, FUZE will award up to four companies a $1 million cash prize each for the program, “which is intended to jumpstart capability development for the second interceptor,” Willis said.
The prize pool is far smaller than the funding required to build the IFPC Increment 2 interceptors currently being developed. Lockheed Martin and a Boeing-Anduril team were recently selected to move onto the second phase of the initial competition, but Willis clarified that while FUZE tech could feed into the larger Army IFPC Inc 2 program, the two are separate for now.
“We’re executing this [FUZE] competition to see if we can incentivize or identify novel technology approaches to meet this mission. So this is in parallel,” he said. “If successful at the end, there will be an opportunity to integrate within the broader program of record, but the vendors that were selected for IFPC Inc 2 second interceptor are moving along their way.”
Apart from the low-cost interceptor competition, Willis said there are other larger acquisition issues FUZE plans to tackle in FY27, but declined to share them as he said they are “not fully baked.”
“I’d say we’ve moved away from the prior acquisition methodology of spending years, if not decades, developing some bespoke, eloquent solution that really didn’t work in the field to recognizing that we need to move quickly and take risks to make sure that our soldiers have access to the best technology,” Willis said.

articles.title: Drones and autonomous warfare: ‘One-way attack’ and reshaping ISR
articles.snippet: [Sponsored] Systems that can work independently while still being part of a unit are critical to carrying out multi-domain operations.
articles.full_text:
Whether it’s seaborne reconnaissance platforms such as the Global Autonomous Reconnaissance Craft (GARC) – now called LYNX – or semi-submersible logistics such as AEVEX Maritime Systems’ NightTrain or high-flying drones providing ISR, autonomous systems are playing a growing role in multi-domain missions, offering longer time on site, greater coverage in contested areas and carrying out missions without putting crew members in harm’s way.
Breaking Defense spoke with Craig Anders, SVP of Growth at AEVEX, about the need for autonomy, how the company is building multi-domain solutions and lessons learned from the use of uncrewed systems in Ukraine and Iran.
What’s the threat scenario right now that is driving the need for air and maritime autonomy?
Anders: We’re operating under this environment with persistent surveillance, ships, comms, everything’s exposed to attack. Everybody can see everything everywhere. Adversaries are out there deploying inexpensive systems at volume, at scale, and it disrupts the navigation and communications that we depend on to fight. GPS is a mess, comms are a mess, everything’s being jammed.
By creating the distributed capability to help grow reach and reduce the exposure of the manned side of things, both air and maritime autonomy can help maintain awareness, mission effects and keep the forces operating across way larger areas and swaths of the area of responsibility (AOR). These systems need to remain useful when navigation and communications are degraded and operating conditions change.
It’s such a dynamic battlefield these days that having autonomy that doesn’t rely on traditional methods of fighting is now this situation that is critical to mission success.
How have the lessons learned from Ukraine and Iran shaped the thinking around air and maritime autonomy?
We’ve learned both what to do and what not to do over the past four to five years. I was in the military and we started off the Phoenix Ghost program on the government side, and I was able to come here and continue that mission. One of the things we learned there is if you can’t cycle fast, if you don’t have people on the ground near the fight, you’re going to get left behind because being able to dynamically flex, have short engineering cycles, short stroke changes to systems outside the normal build process, you’re just going to lose.
Iran reinforces that pressure. They mass inexpensive threats on the battlefield. They levy pressure on our defenses, our inventories and our maritime access at a level we’ve never seen before. Affordability is key. Resilience of the system is key. Being able to adapt to keep it all working together is the only way to succeed in this environment.
We need functional systems in a degraded environment. We need to be able to have close connections between the operators and the engineers, and our production approach needs to be flexible enough to incorporate those changes fast. Otherwise, we’re not going to have what we need to fight. Even if we do deliver it, it’s not going to be very effective. We strive to shorten those engineering cycles, shorten those production cycles and continue to get users the things they need in a short timeline.
That’s because the Research, Development, Test, and Evaluation, RDT&E, cycle has to move at the pace of combat.
Right, and here’s the deal. Over time, airplanes aren’t going to grow extra wings or weird new kinds of propellers. This becomes largely an autonomy and a software fight. You have to have a good solid vehicle by which to implement these capabilities, whether it’s air, sea or subsea.
We’re taking the background we have in airborne intelligence, ISR, one-way attack and what we’ve learned on the battlefield, and producing that in a method that ties up with the way the US wants to fight.
What is evolving rapidly is how the US employs affordable unmanned systems at scale, across domains and as part of a broader force. That requires more than platforms. It requires concepts of operations, force structure, storage, forward support, and sustainment that keep those systems effective as conditions change.
What multi-domain capabilities are needed, and how has AEVEX evolved into a company that can offer them?
A key to this coming fight is understanding what layered defense and offense looks like. You don’t want to just send a couple long-range, one-way assets out there. They’ll probably just get shot down and you won’t know what happened. You don’t want to have a USV just floating out there in the water by itself. You want these things working together autonomously, but also passing information back to be used for the rest of the fight. Ultimately, this whole multi-domain concept is important to ensuring mission success in these AORs because of the uncertainty.
We believe that bringing in this BlackSea piece – there’s one-way attack boats, ISR boats, security, there’s mine sweeping. You have high-flying ISR assets that work with the boats. You have one-way attack that gets tied together by the boats on the water and the planes in the sky.
When you bring systems together to accomplish different parts of a mission, a common autonomy architecture and compatible interfaces can help them share information and coordinate more effectively. That is the opportunity we are pursuing across air, surface, and subsea capabilities. Our CompassX family of navigation and autonomy capabilities supports that approach, with modular hardware and software tailored to the platform and mission.
There are so many different capabilities you can bring to bear using these types of systems, whether it’s ISR, non-kinetic effects, EW/EA, mine sweeping, mine neutralization, critical infrastructure protection, long-range logistics. There’s so much you can bring to bear that helps take people out of harm’s way, but still accomplish the mission set. When you start to tie all these together across our divisions, it tells a story and sets a new standard on the battlefield.
How does having all of these systems working in conjunction give a more comprehensive picture of the battlefield to decision makers?
You’re going to see things you couldn’t see before. You’re going to see patterns develop. Every platform the military owns, operates or uses generates data, and that data, a lot of times, largely goes unused. As you start to pull together these systems of systems and these whole concepts of operations, you start to see different points where you can pull and utilize data to help make better decisions, target better, communicate better, share data across multiple common operating pictures, and enable the fighting man to make better decisions across the board.
You mentioned BlackSea Technologies, which you recently acquired and is now AEVEX Maritime Systems. What capabilities do they bring?
AEVEX already had surface capabilities through Mako. Our Maritime Systems division adds substantially greater maritime engineering, vessel manufacturing, and operational depth. That broadens both our portfolio and the expertise we can bring to customers.
When you look at their main system, it used to be called the GARC, now it’s LYNX. That’s a US Navy Program of Record. We’ve delivered 350 vessels, and now we’re revamping them to increase the comm/nav solution on it to make it even more adaptable in the current environment.
Those systems are fantastic. They’re all aluminum. We have more than 25,000 operational hours in them. They’re doing mine sweeping in the straits right now. They’re doing countermeasures. They have some unique reconfigurable capabilities that a lot of other people do not. Affordability is also central to our approach.
When you look at that, coupled with some of the other things we’re doing such as the NightTrain, low visibility container transport and delivery; that’s a semi-submersible, large ship, has a couple storage containers on the back. It has a wet bay and it does 2,700 nautical miles.
We have the sea-based petroleum distribution, which is a tanker that holds 185,000 gallons of gas that you can sink down to the sea floor and cache petroleum in place for contingency operations. It creates just a whole other level of how you would operate and fight in that environment.
What else should people know about AEVEX and what you’re doing in the field?
The biggest thing is multi-domain matters, because every mission out there crosses multiple domains. Bringing air, surface, and subsea capabilities together is going to give the warfighter what they need and create opportunities for more coordinated operations. It’s hard to fight in a vacuum. If you’re just focused on air, you’re just focused on sea, you’re missing out. You’re missing out on the CONOPS that help you win effectively and spend less doing it.
Autonomy is changing the way forces see and operate and deliver effects, sustain themselves. Autonomy is bringing capability to bear. Autonomy is also the back side, where you’re using data to analyze and grow your models in an effort to continue to iterate these systems to success. Its value is in real-world performance and real-world operating conditions, but you take that back and you grow your systems based on data and not conjecture. That’s exciting for me.
We bring substantial operational experience delivering and supporting these capabilities. That experience gives us a strong foundation for incorporating lessons from the field and continually improving our systems as requirements evolve. The production process has to keep pace as well, so we can move those improvements into repeatable builds and deliver them at the volume customers need.
That’s what we’re building at AEVEX: the ability to turn evolving mission requirements into capability customers can field and use. We help customers develop concepts of operations, integrate capabilities, and sustain them in the field. That is how we deliver solutions that remain useful as the mission changes.

articles.title: Ideal Aerosmith debuts ‘Troublemaker’ for one-way attack
articles.snippet: The company is aiming to tackle a “sweet spot” in the strike market with the Group 3 Troublemaker, and has a “sponsor” in the US Navy, according to executive David Markert.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The small firm Ideal Aerosmith is pivoting to defense, debuting an in-house developed attack drone in a bid to capitalize on surging interest in low-cost munitions.
Founded in 1938, North Dakota-based Ideal Aerosmith — not to be confused with the name of your favorite playlist — has undergone a few “instantiations” throughout its decades-long history, David Markert, the company’s senior vice president and general manager of government systems, told Breaking Defense in an Oct. 2 interview. The firm has been “defense adjacent” in more recent years, Markert said, manufacturing test equipment for navigation systems.
But about three years ago amid rising demand for defense tech, Ideal Aerosmith decided to pursue military customers directly, according to Markert. The company chose a low-cost, one-way attack drone, now dubbed “Troublemaker,” and publicly unveiled the system Thursday as a chief platform to market to prospective customers.
Ideal is now entering low-rate production for the Troublemaker, according to Markert, who said the company has a “Department of the Navy sponsor” for the system when asked about current contracts. He said the company has built 26 of Troublemakers so far, and is manufacturing the drones at a rate of two per week. With sufficient demand, he added the company could build up to 20 Troublemakers weekly within existing infrastructure.
“We felt that was a sweet spot in the market,” Markert said of a one-way attack drone. “And as the market turned away from exquisite systems to low-cost, affordable mass, it seemed like the ideal time to go after that. Given our engineering pedigree [and] our precision manufacturing, it gave us a pretty solid base to transfer some of those skills over to building drones.”
With a 15-foot wingspan, the Troublemaker is classified as a Group 3 system and can be launched from a catapult or truck. The company says the drone can fly in swarms, boasts a range of over 750 nautical miles (863 miles), has an endurance time exceeding 10 hours and can carry a payload of 30 pounds for missions spanning attack to reconnaissance.
Markert said the company views the Troublemaker as filling a different niche compared to other strike options, particularly amid surging interest in low-cost cruise missiles. He argued key differences, like the ability to reuse the drone — which can be recovered via a skid landing — and the system’s ability to launch without the need for more specialized infrastructure or platforms, such as aircraft.
“We looked at the air launch or the palletized launch,” he said. “There’s a ton of guys in that low-cost cruise missile space. We’re differentiated from that because we’re in the drone space, and in our definition of that, drones give you post-flight options that missiles don’t give you.”
Troublemaker is not the company’s only planned defense product. Markert said Ideal is also working on other systems with greater range and payload capacity. But for the time being, there are more immediate concerns, like the effects of a continuing resolution (CR) that began Oct. 1 and freezes new-start programs while holding funding at prior-year levels.
Ideal has thrown its hat into the ring for relevant solicitations, Markert said, but added that “clearly, the CR has impact.”
“How much of an impact it has, we don’t know at this point. We’re kind of keeping our fingers crossed and holding our breath that this stuff was funded under the [fiscal 2026] budget,” he said.

articles.title: Thales looks to export new C2 platform to Gulf nations, says executive
articles.snippet: “We do believe that there is an operational need and a solution based on our open standard, being able to address the sovereignty for the countries. We do believe that this solution is already fit for purpose regarding the Gulf,” Thales Vice President for Multi-Domain Operations Patrick Moreau told Breaking Defense.
articles.full_text:
BEIRUT — French aerospace and defense giant Thales is pitching its new artificial intelligence-enabled command and control system, dubbed HexaForce, as a solution specifically for the Gulf market, a top executive told Breaking Defense.
“We do believe that there is an operational need and a solution based on our open standard, being able to address the sovereignty for the countries. We do believe that this solution is already fit for purpose regarding the Gulf,” Thales Vice President for Multi-Domain Operations Patrick Moreau said in an interview Tuesday.
Moreau declined to comment on any discussions the company may be having with individual Middle East customers.
Unveiled Sept. 17, HexaForce is designed to “accelerate decision-making and secure operational advantage at every level of command” for “NATO and allied nations,” the company’s release explains.
“This solution is a data, AI-powered solution. We leverage on the AI to develop quite fast, and there is agentic and LLM [large language model] inside this solution [that] could really allow the end users, for instance, to propose targeting solution to the operator, meaning that it allows the operator to process a huge amount of data,” Moreau said.
He added that HexaForce is based on open-source data, allowing users to reinforce sovereign capability within the state. This means, Moreau explained, if “you understand how it has been built and you could adapt the solution for the local needs. The [operational] data remains the property of the nation, meaning that it will remain within the country, guaranteeing the sovereignty of the solution.”
Thales says the platform also covers both strategic- and tactical-level decision making. While the C2 platform has yet to be deployed in any conflict, it has been tested in military exercises like the CWIX NATO exercise that took place in June in Poland.
The live-trial phases of HexaForce will forge a path for “for full-scale deployment, targeting an increase in capacity from 100 to 1,000 targets processed per day,” Thales’ release states.
Regarding the possibility of coproduction of this system with Gulf states in compliance with localization efforts in the region, Moreau answered, “whenever we deploy it locally, we could rely on domestic capabilities of Thales and/or partners to develop AI-powered capability, which are much more sovereign, considered as sovereign eyes only by the country.”
Gulf states like Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates and Qatar have stressed local production in recent years according to national mandates.

articles.title: Japan confirms arrest of Russian Qilin operative, extradition to Germany
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Japan’s National Police Agency confirmed the arrest and extradition to Germany of a Russian national accused of being involved in the Qilin ransomware gang.
articles.full_text:
Japan confirms arrest of Russian Qilin operative, extradition to Germany
Japan’s National Police Agency confirmed on Thursday the arrest and extradition of a Russian national accused of being involved in the Qilin ransomware gang.
Japanese officials said they received an arrest warrant from Germany for the 28-year-old Russian national, whose name was not released, for their alleged role in a ransomware attack on a German company. Japan’s Ministry of Justice worked to detain the suspect before they were extradited to Germany.
The news outlet Nippon reported that the operation began in May when officials learned the suspect planned to come to Japan for vacation. He was arrested at a hotel in Osaka that month and sent to Germany in June. German law enforcement did not respond to requests for comment.
The Qilin ransomware gang has been behind dozens of high-profile attacks, including incidents in both Germany and Japan.
The group took credit for an April ransomware attack on German democratic socialist political party Die Linke and another devastating incident last year involving Japanese beverage giant Asahi.
Asahi spent weeks recovering from the attack, which disrupted its order processing, shipping, and customer services. The attackers also leaked Asahi’s financial records, employee data, contracts and development forecasts.
The group faced increased law enforcement scrutiny in 2024 after an attack on a British healthcare company that prompted major disruptions to medical services. It quickly returned with attacks on the government of Palau and one of the largest newspaper chains in the U.S..
Qilin was one of the most active ransomware operations in 2025. targeting Kuala Lumpur International Airport, the Texas city of Sugar Land, and more.
The group has continued to launch damaging attacks in 2026, with researchers saying it was the second most active ransomware gang in July with 127 reported attacks. French rugby club Stade Français Paris confirmed it had been attacked after being added to Qilin’s leak site.
In August, Qilin actors took credit for a ransomware attack on the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF). The group allegedly stole information about targets of ATF investigations.

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands impacted by data breach at biosensor firm iRhythm
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: A company known for wearable cardiac sensors, iRhythm, has begun notifying states of the impact of a data breach from the summer.
articles.full_text:
Hundreds of thousands impacted by data breach at biosensor firm iRhythm
Medical device maker iRhythm said the data of at least 360,000 people was breached in a June cyberattack.
The company began filing breach notices in multiple states this week, telling regulators and victims that the incident occurred on June 8 and involved unauthorized access to third-party systems.
iRhythm is best known for Zio Patch — a sensor that patients wear on their chest for long-term continuous cardiac monitoring and heart arrhythmia detection.
The company said 298,647 people in Texas had information stolen alongside another 69,526 in South Carolina. iRhythm also filed breach notices in California.
A company spokesperson declined to say the full number of victims, telling Recorded Future News that iRhythm “responded promptly after detecting the unauthorized access and, once the scope was verified, notified affected individuals and applicable regulators.”
“The incident did not affect iRhythm clinical systems or medical devices and did not result in a loss of service or disruption to operations,” the spokesperson said.
An investigation into the incident revealed that hackers had access to company systems between June 3 and June 8. The hackers gained access to unidentified third-party-hosted business applications through a social engineering attack.
The information stolen includes names, addresses, phone numbers, iRhythm patient account numbers, iRhythm device serial numbers, patient insurance numbers, dates of service, and date of birth.
The cybercriminals accessed and downloaded the information, according to a statement from iRhythm. The company said it has “no evidence that any personal information has been or will be used to commit identity theft.” No hacking group ever publicly took credit for the attack.
The cyberattack did not impact the company’s products, devices, manufacturing process or distribution operations — and iRhythm said its finances were not disturbed. The company reported $224.2 million in Q2 revenue.
In a June 8-K filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), iRhythm said it “received communications from a threat actor claiming to have obtained sensitive information, including proprietary data, patient protected health information and other personal information.”
“The communications from the threat actor demanded payment in exchange for not publicly disclosing this information,” the company said.
“Since receipt of the communications, the Company has confirmed that certain data was exfiltrated from those applications.”
Medical device companies have been battered by cybercriminals over the last two years, with dozens experiencing cybersecurity incidents that impacted crucial business and manufacturing systems.
Cyberattacks on Medtronic, Boston Scientific, Stryker, UFP, Masimo, Surmodics, Artivion and Zoll have leaked the sensitive medical data of millions and caused supply chain issues.
